source_text: Ὥσπερ δὲ κτῆμα τὸ ἐξ ἁρπαγῆς βλαβερώτατον καὶ ἀνοσιώτατον, οὕτω καὶ ἀνδρὶ ἐπιθυμητῇ χρημάτων οὐκ ἐκγίνεται κόρος, οὔθ᾽ ἡ παρὰ τῶν πέλας εὔνοια· κἂν ὁτιοῦν μάλιστα πάμπολυ ἀργύριον ἐπικτήσωνται. Τοῦτο μὲν γὰρ μάταιον. Ἀγαθότης δὲ τοὺς συνόντας αὐτῇ ὑπερευφραίνουσα, ἀνδρείους ἀπεργάζεται τοῦ καθορᾶν ἕκαστα τῶν πραγμάτων παρέχουσα τὴν δύναμιν. Μέγα δὲ καὶ τὸ μὴ προστετηκέναι τοιαύταις φροντίσιν· ὁ μέν γε πένης, κἂν δοῦλος ᾖ, καὶ μὴ ὑπερεμπλήσας τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γαστέρα, προσηνοῦς μεταλαμβάνει τῆς διὰ τοῦ ὕπνου ἀνέσεως· πλούτου δὲ ἐπιθυμία σύνεστι ἀγρυπνίαις καὶ καμάτοις ψυχῆς. Τί δ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο τούτου ἀτοπώτερον, ἢ τὸ μετὰ πολλῆς σπουδῆς καὶ ἐπιμελείας ἀποθησαυρίζοντα τὸν πλοῦτον συντηρεῖν, μυρίων ἑαυτῷ φυλάσσοντα κακῶν ἀφορμήν; Καὶ τὸν πλοῦτον ἐκεῖνον ἀνάγκη ἀπολέσθαι ποτὲ καὶ διαφθαρῆναι, εἴτε γένοιτο τῷ κτησαμένῳ τέκνα, εἴτε καὶ μή· αὐτόν τε εἰ καὶ μὴ βούλοιτο προσήκει τοιοῦτον εἰς τὴν γῆν πεσεῖν καὶ ἀπελθεῖν, οἷος καὶ ὁπότε εἰς τὸ εἶναι παρὼν ἐτύγχανε. Κεναῖς δὲ χερσὶν ἀπιέναι μέλλων, αὔξει τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κακίαν, ὥσπερ οὐκ ἐνθυμούμενος, ὅτι ἐπίκειται αὐτῷ τέλος τοῦ βίου τῇ γενέσει ὅμοιον, καὶ ὅτι ἀνόνητα μοχθεῖ, εἰς δέ τινα μᾶλλον ἀνέμου ὁρμήν, ἤπερ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ σπουδῇ χαριζόμενος, καταναλώσας τὸν ἑαυτοῦ βίον σύμπαντα, ἔν τε ἐπιθυμίαις ἀνοσιωτάταις, καὶ ἐν ὁρμαῖς ἀλόγοις, ἔτι δὲ λύπαις καὶ ἀρρωστίαις. Καὶ συνελόντι φάναι, σκότος μέν εἰσι τῷ τοιούτῳ αἱ ἡμέραι· πένθος δὲ ἡ ζωή. Ἀγαθόν γε μὴν ἐκεῖνο καὶ οὐκ ἀπόβλητον· Θεοῦ γάρ ἐστι δῶρον, τὸ δυνηθῆναι ἀπολαῦσαι ἄνθρωπον τῶν ἑαυτοῦ καματῶν ἐν εὐφροσύνῃ, θεόσδοτα, καὶ οὐχ ἁρπακτικὰ δεξάμενον κτήματα. Οὔτε γὰρ λύπαις οὖτός γε νοσεῖ, οὔτε ὡς ἐπὶ πολὺ ἐνθυμήσεσι πονηραῖς δουλεύει· συμμετρεῖται δὲ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ βίον εὐποιίαις τοῖς πᾶσιν εὐθυμούμενος, καὶ ἀγαλλιώμενος τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ δωρεᾷ.
thought_title: The harm of greed and the good of enjoying one's labor as God's gift
orientation: Solomon, as reported by Gregory, teaches that greed is like stolen goods—utterly harmful—while contentment in one's work comes from God and brings peace.
pass_a_gloss: Just as property taken by robbery is most harmful and most impious, so also to a man desirous of wealth no satiety comes forth, nor the goodwill of those nearby; even if they acquire anything at all, most especially very much silver. For this is futile. But goodness, making those who associate with it exceedingly glad, works out brave men, providing the power to look upon each of the matters. Great also is the not having been added to such cares; for the poor man, even if he is a slave, and not having overfilled his own stomach, partakes pleasantly of the relief through sleep; but desire of wealth is companion to sleeplessness and toils of soul. What then would happen more out of place than this, than the with much zeal and care treasuring up the wealth to preserve it, guarding for himself occasion of ten thousand evils? And that wealth is necessary to be lost sometime and to be corrupted, whether children should happen to the acquirer, or even not; himself also even if he would not wish it, it is fitting such a one to fall into the earth and to depart, of what sort also whenever he happened to be present for the being. Being about to depart with empty hands, he increases his own badness, as if not considering that there lies upon him an end of life similar to the birth, and that he toils uselessly, into a certain impulse of wind rather, gratifying his own zeal, having consumed his whole life both in most impious desires, and in irrational impulses, still moreover in griefs and sicknesses. And to speak summarily, darkness are the days to such a man; grief is the life. Good indeed however is that, and not to be thrown away; for it is a gift of God, the to be able a man to enjoy his own labors in gladness, God-given things, and not rapacious ones having received possessions. For neither with griefs does this man ail, nor for a long time with wicked thoughts does he serve; but he measures out his own life with good deeds toward all, being of good cheer, and exulting in the gift of God.

lemmas.gloss: more out of place, more absurd

choices.why: Literal rendering of the noun phrase; 'property' for κτῆμα, 'taken by robbery' for τὸ ἐξ ἁρπαγῆς.
Participle/dative construction describing the person; 'wealth' for χρημάτων (genitive plural).
ἀπεργάζομαι = produce, work out; ἀνδρείους = brave men (accusative plural).
Compound adjective θεός + δότος; glossary sense for 'gift of God' language.
ἄλογος = without reason/logos; ὁρμή = impulse, drive.

choices.english: he measures out his own life with good deeds
choices.why: συμμετρέομαι middle = measure out for oneself; εὐποιίαις = good deeds/benefactions (dative plural).
rejected: he proportions his life by good works
he orders his life with kindnesses

bible_refs.note: Greedy man never satisfied; wealth brings sleeplessness; laborer's sleep is sweet.
Riches hoarded to owner's hurt; lost in misfortune; depart naked; eat in darkness.
Good to eat, drink, enjoy labor—gift of God; God keeps him occupied with gladness.

pass_b_english: Just as property taken by robbery is the most harmful and most impious thing a person can possess, so a man desirous of wealth never gets his fill, nor does he win the goodwill of those around him, even if he acquires a vast amount of silver. That is futile. Goodness, on the other hand, makes those who share in it exceedingly glad and produces brave men, giving them the power to look clearly at every circumstance. It is also a great thing to be free of such anxieties. For even a poor man, even if he is a slave and has not overfilled his own belly, enjoys the pleasant relief that comes through sleep. But the desire for wealth goes hand in hand with sleeplessness and toils of the soul. What could be more absurd than a man who, with great eagerness and care, hoards his wealth to preserve it, while keeping for himself the source of countless evils? That wealth must eventually be lost and destroyed, whether the owner has children or not. And even if he would not wish it, he himself must fall into the earth and depart, just as he was when he came into being. When he is about to leave with empty hands, he increases his own wickedness, as if forgetting that the end of his life lies upon him, similar to his birth, and that he toils uselessly, surrendering his whole life to the impulse of wind rather than to his own earnest effort, consuming it in utterly impious desires, in irrational impulses, and furthermore in sorrows and sicknesses. To sum up: for such a man his days are darkness, and his life is mourning. But that other thing is good and not to be thrown away: it is a gift of God for a human being to be able to enjoy his own labors with gladness, receiving God-given possessions, not ones taken by robbery. For that man is not sick with sorrows, nor is he, for the most part, enslaved to wicked thoughts; he measures out his own life with good deeds, remaining cheerful toward all, and exulting in the gift of God.

problems.quote: while guarding against a myriad of occasions for evil
problems.why: The man keeps and stores up for himself countless occasions of evil. The English reverses this into guarding against them.
problems.fix: while keeping for himself the source of countless evils?

problems.quote: never finds satisfaction, not even from the goodwill of those around him
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἐκγίνεται κόρος, οὔθ᾽ ἡ παρὰ τῶν πέλας εὔνοια
problems.why: The source says neither satisfaction nor his neighbors' goodwill comes to him. The English treats goodwill as a possible source of satisfaction.
problems.fix: never gets his fill, nor does he win the goodwill of those around him,

problems.quote: nor does he serve wicked thoughts for a long time
problems.source_quote: οὔτε ὡς ἐπὶ πολὺ ἐνθυμήσεσι πονηραῖς δουλεύει
problems.why: ὡς ἐπὶ πολύ means for the most part, not for a long time.
problems.fix: nor is he, for the most part, enslaved to wicked thoughts
problems.ruling: ὡς ἐπὶ πολύ means 'for the most part/generally', not duration. 'For a long time' changes the claim about how often he serves wicked thoughts.

edits.old: while guarding against a myriad of occasions for evil
edits.new: while keeping for himself the source of countless evils

edits.old: never finds satisfaction, not even from the goodwill of those around him
edits.new: never gets his fill, nor does he win the goodwill of those around him

edits.old: nor does he serve wicked thoughts for a long time
edits.new: nor is he, for the most part, enslaved to wicked thoughts

fixed: Corrected 'guarding against' to 'keeping for himself the source of' to match μυρίων ἑαυτῷ φυλάσσοντα κακῶν ἀφορμήν (guarding for himself occasion/source of ten thousand evils).

Corrected 'never finds satisfaction, not even from the goodwill of those around him' to 'never gets his fill, nor does he win the goodwill of those around him' to match οὐκ ἐκγίνεται κόρος, οὔθ᾽ ἡ παρὰ τῶν πέλας εὔνοια (no satiety comes forth, nor the goodwill of those nearby).

Corrected 'nor does he serve wicked thoughts for a long time' to 'nor is he, for the most part, enslaved to wicked thoughts' to match οὔτε ὡς ἐπὶ πολὺ ἐνθυμήσεσι πονηραῖς δουλεύει (nor for the most part does he serve wicked thoughts).

last_rejected.quote: surrendering his whole life to the impulse of wind rather than to his own earnest effort, consuming it in utterly impious desires
last_rejected.source_quote: εἰς δέ τινα μᾶλλον ἀνέμου ὁρμήν, ἤπερ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ σπουδῇ χαριζόμενος, καταναλώσας τὸν ἑαυτοῦ βίον σύμπαντα, ἔν τε ἐπιθυμίαις ἀνοσιωτάταις
last_rejected.why: His whole life is spent in desires, impulses, grief, and sickness; the wind is only where his useless toil goes, rather than gratifying his own effort.
last_rejected.fix: and that he toils uselessly, rather into some rush of wind than gratifying his own earnest effort, having spent his whole life in utterly impious desires, irrational impulses, sorrows, and sicknesses.
last_rejected.ruling: The English keeps the sense of χαριζόμενος (gratifying wind rather than his own σπουδῇ) and καταναλώσας τὸν βίον σύμπαντα in desires and impulses. The 'surrendering his life' phrasing is a loose nuance, not a changed meaning.
